claims.text: Dr. Brian Eastridge is a trauma surgeon and chief of the Division of Trauma and Emergency Surgery at UT Health San Antonio.
claims.quote: Brian Eastridge, MD, is a clinical professor of surgery, chief of the Division of Trauma and Emergency Surgery, and holds the Jocelyn and Joe Straus Endowed Chair in Trauma Research. Eastridge is a trauma surgeon at UT Health San Antonio.

claims.text: Texas EMS and trauma registry data show up to 80 percent of the most severely injured patients wait more than two hours for transfer to a trauma center.
claims.quote: In Texas, state EMS and trauma registry data shows up to 80% of the most severely injured patients wait more than two hours to be transferred to a trauma center.

claims.text: With the tool, the transfer decision could take five to 10 minutes, against a current standard of 15 to 30.
claims.quote: Transfer decision could be made in five to 10 minutes, though the current standard is 15 to 30.

claims.text: Eastridge says the tool pushes the doctor to make the transfer call earlier.
claims.quote: "It pushes the doctor to make that decision and make that transfer call earlier," he said, "rather than trying to specifically identify injury patterns or specific injuries prior to the patient's transfer."

claims.text: Eastridge co-leads iRemedyACT, a statewide research consortium using AI to close the transfer delay.
claims.quote: Eastridge co-leads iRemedyACT, a statewide research consortium using artificial intelligence to close that gap.

claims.text: The pilot has supplemental funding from what TPR calls the UT System's AI Beacon Moonshot program.
claims.quote: With supplemental funding from the UT System's AI Beacon Moonshot program, Eastridge said the team plans to launch a statewide pilot of the decision-support tool this fall.

claims.text: As of September 13th, 2026, the team planned a statewide pilot of the decision-support tool that fall.
claims.quote: Eastridge said the team plans to launch a statewide pilot of the decision-support tool this fall.

claims.text: The tool flags severe injury patterns and prompts an earlier transfer call, sharpening rather than replacing the doctor's judgment.
claims.quote: It wouldn’t replace the doctor's judgment, he explained, but sharpen it. The tool his team is developing flags severe injury patterns and prompts an earlier transfer call.

claims.text: An EMS crew often takes the patient to the nearest facility, frequently a Level Four trauma center, which is a well-equipped rural ER without dedicated trauma surgeons on call.
claims.quote: An EMS crew picks up a patient and takes them to the nearest facility, often a Level Four trauma center, essentially a well-equipped rural emergency room without dedicated trauma surgeons on call.

claims.text: If a transfer is needed, the rural doctor has to hospital shop for a trauma center that will take the patient and call an ambulance.
claims.quote: Then, if a transfer is needed, "they have to hospital shop to find a trauma center that will take the patient" and call an ambulance to carry it out.

claims.text: Rural ER doctors treat everything from strokes to pediatric flu, and their communities see little injury, so trauma is rarely their strength.
claims.quote: Rural ER doctors treat everything from strokes to pediatric flu, he noted, and trauma isn't usually their specialty. "Trauma is generally not one of their specific strong sets, because generally these rural communities don't see a lot of injury."

claims.text: Trauma is the leading cause of death for people up to age 45.
claims.quote: Trauma is the leading cause of death for people up to age 45.

claims.text: Eastridge suspects a faster decision would bring a significant survival benefit for the severely injured.
claims.quote: Closing that gap, he believes, could save lives. “Particularly for the severely injured patients,” he said. “We suspect there would be a significant survival benefit.”

claims.text: Eastridge compares the AI to an ultrasound, one more tool in the clinical toolbox.
claims.quote: "It is just a tool," he said. "You don't use your ultrasound and exclusively make your decisions with that ultrasound. I think we should consider this today as just another tool in our clinical toolbox to actually get at making the right decision for the patient."

claims.text: Eastridge spent much of his career as an Army trauma surgeon in war zones.
claims.quote: Dr. Brian Eastridge has spent much of his career as an Army trauma surgeon in war zones, and that experience shapes how he sees his current job as chief of the Division of Trauma and Emergency Surgery at UT Health San Antonio.

claims.text: Eastridge describes the work as meeting people on the worst days of their lives.
claims.quote: "We tend to meet people on the worst days of their lives," Eastridge said. "It's very, very high stakes."

claims.text: iRemedyACT stands for Identification and Remediation of Delays to Definitive Care of Critically Injured Patients in the Texas Trauma System.
claims.quote: iRemedyACT is tortured shorthand for Identification and Remediation of Delays to Definitive Care of Critically Injured Patients in the Texas Trauma System with Advances in AI to Improve Care for Trauma.

claims.text: The project began with a one million dollar grant from the UT System's Trauma Research and Combat Casualty Care Collaborative.
claims.quote: The project received a million dollars for this research from the Trauma Research and Combat Casualty Care Collaborative of The University of Texas System.

claims.text: BEACON is an 18-month, $500,000 pilot to test AI for trauma and stroke care across UT sites and their rural partners.
claims.quote: Over the 18-month, $500,000 pilot project, BEACON will test, deploy and scale AI innovations designed to improve emergency care decision-making and outcomes for trauma and stroke patients across UT sites and their rural partners.

claims.text: BEACON stands for Bedside Emergency AI for Care Orchestration and won an AI Moonshot Innovation Award from UT REAL Health AI.
claims.quote: the team received an inaugural AI Moonshot Innovation Award from the UT REAL Health AI program to launch BEACON — Bedside Emergency AI for Care Orchestration.

claims.text: Three moonshot projects each received up to $500,000.
claims.quote: Three moonshot projects each received up to $500,000 to pursue transformative clinical AI.

claims.text: The UT System says BEACON deploys an AI clinical assistant across seven UT hospital sites to optimize emergency triage and transfer decisions.
claims.quote: deploys “Leah,” an AI clinical assistant trained on more than 400,000 trauma cases, across seven UT hospital sites to optimize emergency triage and transfer decisions.

claims.text: UTSA says BEACON's assistant was trained on trauma cases from across Texas, including data from seven UT trauma centers.
claims.quote: During its first nine months, BEACON will test Selja, an AI clinical assistant developed by the team to support emergency triage and transfer decisions. Selja has been trained on more than 1 million trauma cases from across Texas, including prospective data from seven UT hospital system trauma centers.

claims.text: BEACON is not designed to replace physicians.
claims.quote: BEACON is not designed to replace physicians. Instead, the team is building AI to support highly trained clinicians with additional information, context and decision support.

claims.text: Co-investigator Dr. Elizabeth Scherer says the goal is getting patients to the right level of care within the right amount of time.
claims.quote: “In environments with variable resources, the goal is to ensure patients get to the right level of care within the right amount of time.”

claims.text: Texas has 288 designated trauma facilities, 22 of them Level I and 173 basic Level IV, as of October 28th, 2026.
claims.quote: Total number of Designated Trauma Facilities 288 Comprehensive (Level I) 22 facilities currently designated Major (Level II) 31 facilities currently designated Advanced (Level III) 62 facilities currently designated Basic (Level IV) 173 facilities currently designated Designated Facilities By Level These lists are current as of October 28, 2026

claims.text: Texas is divided into 22 Trauma Service Areas, each with a Regional Advisory Council.
claims.quote: whereby the state was divided into twenty-two regions called Trauma Service Areas (Texas Administrative Code § Rule 157.122), provided for the formation of a Regional Advisory Council (Texas Administrative Code § Rule 157.123).

claims.text: The San Antonio regional council's area holds 74 hospitals, two of them Level I trauma centers.
claims.quote: consisting of 74 general and specialty hospitals, including 2 Level I Trauma Centers
